steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using large language models to generate a validation and verification testsuite for OpenACC compilers. Cover what LLMs can do, background on OpenACC and its compilers, why compiler validation is needed and why writing tests by hand is hard, and finish with our contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) can understand natural language input and do tasks based on that understanding. They can do a lot of different tasks, for example text generation, sentiment classification, code generation and document summarization. OpenAI's GPT-4 scored in the 90th percentile on the Uniform Bar Exam and in the 99th percentile on the verbal GRE, and it got several other impressive scores on prestigious academic exams too. Anthropic's Claude 2 also did well, with 76.5% on the multiple choice section of the Bar exam and over 90th percentile on the GRE reading and writing exams. LLMs are pre-trained with self-supervised learning on large datasets that are unlabeled, and they can be fine-tuned with datasets from a specific domain so they perform better on specific tasks. There are also code-specific LLMs which are trained on a large corpus of open-source code like stack overflow and GitHub, and these can write code that is functional and complex, as can be seen in Github Copilot and Codeium.

Because LLMs can do so much, in this paper we look at which LLMs and which prompt engineering techniques are most suitable for generating a validation and verification testsuite for high-performance computing (HPC) compilers, starting from a standard specification that is mostly natural language. The goal is to check whether C/C++/Fortran compiler implementations of the directive-based programming models OpenMP and OpenACC are correct. As far as we know, this paper is the first of its kind. The paper focuses on OpenACC, but the approach can be adapted to OpenMP as well (we are also working on this). How LLMs perform on programming tasks like interview-style questions has been explored in the past couple of years. But nobody has yet applied this to validating compilers based on a standard specification.

OpenACC is a directive-based programming model and it targets x86 architectures, A64FX and accelerators like GPUs. OpenACC is defined by a standard specification. Open-source compilers like GCC and LLVM/Clacc, and vendors like HPE Cray (for Fortran) and NVIDIA, interpret the specification and develop compilers from it. GCC, Clacc and HPE Cray compilers target X86, NVIDIA and AMD accelerator architectures, and NVIDIA compilers target X86, NVIDIA GPUs and A64FX. OpenACC gives users different levels of control over how a program executes and how data flows. The compiler can make the optimization decisions, or the user can customize how data and execution are distributed. This is useful for domain scientists who do not want to re-implement domain applications, which can be complex, in a low-level parallel programming language like CUDA, OpenCL or SYCL. OpenACC is very popular and is used in many domains, for example climate, computational fluid dynamics, nuclear physics and biophysics, and others.

## 1.1 Motivation

Since the programming model is popular, it is critical that compiler implementations compile and execute the code correctly. Why is this hard? Different compiler developers interpret the specification differently, and this often leads to misinterpretations and ambiguities. One of the reasons is that the definitions of the features are complex. Even though a lot of effort goes into improving compilers, they are still prone to issues like inaccuracy, like all other software. There are also compilation failures and execution failures that have to be found and fixed. Also each compiler implementation supports OpenACC to a different level and covers a different part of the specification, for example HPE/Cray only supports Fortran. But the user should not have to deal with these challenges and should not have to tailor how they use the implementations for their applications. So the implementations are expected to be the same at the user's level of abstraction.

- Need validation of compiler implementations
  - functional, corner, regression, stress tests; involved and recurrent
  - our OpenACC V&V testsuite, like our OpenMP testsuite
- Manual test writing is hard
  - challenging, cumbersome, may be incorrect/incomplete; too many combinations of base language and paradigm
  - manual tests; team turnover; lag of three weeks to three months or more (Chandrasekaran, co-author, 10+ years training students)
  - lose continuity, behind on deliverable -> motivation for LLMs to complement manual writing
- What LLMs offer
  - "shift" focus to corner case and stress tests; oversight needed, effort front-loaded
  - adapt tests to new/updated features; translation between languages
- Contributions
  - LLM-generated tests; fine-tuning dataset; evaluation of LLMs, prompt engineering, fine-tuning
  - artifacts on our GitHub

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) can understand natural language input and do tasks based on that understanding. They can do a lot of different tasks, for example text generation, sentiment classification, code generation and document summarization. OpenAI's GPT-4 scored in the 90th percentile on the Uniform Bar Exam and in the 99th percentile on the verbal GRE, and it got several other impressive scores on prestigious academic exams too. There are also code-specific LLMs which are trained on a large corpus of open-source code like stack overflow and GitHub, and these can write code that is functional and complex, as can be seen in Github Copilot and Codeium.

Because LLMs can do so much, in this paper we look at which LLMs and which prompt engineering techniques are most suitable for generating a validation and verification testsuite for high-performance computing (HPC) compilers, starting from a standard specification that is mostly natural language. The goal is to check whether C/C++/Fortran compiler implementations of the directive-based programming models OpenMP and OpenACC are correct. As far as we know, this paper is the first of its kind. The paper focuses on OpenACC, but the approach can be adapted to OpenMP as well (we are also working on this). How LLMs perform on programming tasks like interview-style questions has been explored in the past couple of years. But nobody has yet applied this to validating compilers based on a standard specification.

OpenACC is a directive-based programming model and it targets x86 architectures, A64FX and accelerators like GPUs. OpenACC is defined by a standard specification. Open-source compilers like GCC and LLVM/Clacc, and vendors like HPE Cray (for Fortran) and NVIDIA, interpret the specification and develop compilers from it. GCC, Clacc and HPE Cray compilers target X86, NVIDIA and AMD accelerator architectures, and NVIDIA compilers target X86, NVIDIA GPUs and A64FX. OpenACC gives users different levels of control over how a program executes and how data flows. The compiler can make the optimization decisions, or the user can customize how data and execution are distributed. This is useful for domain scientists who do not want to re-implement domain applications, which can be complex, in a low-level parallel programming language like CUDA, OpenCL or SYCL. OpenACC is very popular and is used in many domains, for example climate, computational fluid dynamics, nuclear physics and biophysics, and others.

## 1.1 Motivation

Since the programming model is popular, it is critical that compiler implementations compile and execute the code correctly. Why is this hard? Different compiler developers interpret the specification differently, and this often leads to misinterpretations and ambiguities. One of the reasons is that the definitions of the features are complex. Even though a lot of effort goes into improving compilers, they are still prone to issues like inaccuracy, like all other software. There are also compilation failures and execution failures that have to be found and fixed. Also each compiler implementation supports OpenACC to a different level and covers a different part of the specification, for example HPE/Cray only supports Fortran. But the user should not have to deal with these challenges and should not have to tailor how they use the implementations for their applications. So the implementations are expected to be the same at the user's level of abstraction.

These challenges mean that the compiler implementations need to be validated. This can be done by writing functional, corner, regression and stress tests, which is an involved task that has to be done again and again. We have been developing a validation and verification (V&V) testsuite for OpenACC, the same way we have been developing a testsuite for OpenMP.

Designing the tests can be very challenging and cumbersome, and the tests still may not always be correct or complete. The features of the base language (C, C++, or Fortran) and the parallel programming paradigm (OpenACC or OpenMP) can be used together in many ways, and it is humanely impossible to cover all of them. The tests in both testsuites are created manually, so the teams have to keep up with generating and maintaining tests. Team members change during the project. When members leave and new members are trained to create quality tests there is a lag, which can be from three weeks to three months or more at times. This observation comes from Chandrasekaran's (co-author) experience training undergrad and graduate students to work on parallel computing projects over 10+ years. This can harm the project because we lose continuity and fall behind on deliverable. These hardships are the motivation for this work, where we explore whether LLMs can be used for a V&V testsuite to complement writing these tests manually.

Developers can then "shift" focus to designing complicated corner case tests and stress testing compiler implementations. LLMs need oversight but can be handy if the effort is front-loaded. LLMs can also help adapt an existing test to new or updated features and they do well at translating between languages. LLMs offer many things to developers, but they must be used with human oversight and caution.

The contributions of this paper are:

- 1. LLM-generated tests to check the correctness of OpenACC compiler implementations

- 2. A fine-tuning dataset for this task

- 3. An evaluation of LLMs, prompt engineering techniques and fine-tuning on test generation for OpenACC

The generated testsuites, prompts, fine-tuning dataset, and specification JSON from this paper are available at our GitHub.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are capable of understanding natural language as input and performing tasks with that understanding. LLMs can perform an array of tasks, from text generation to sentiment classification, code generation, document summarization, and more. OpenAI's GPT-4 scored 90th percentile on the Uniform Bar Exam and 99th percentile on the verbal GRE [1], among several other impressive scores on prestigious academic exams. Similarly, Anthropic's Claude 2 achieved a 76.5% score on the multiple choice section of the Bar exam, and over 90th percentile on GRE reading and writing exams [2]. LLMs are pre-trained on large, unlabeled datasets with self-supervised learning and can be fine-tuned with domain-specific datasets for improved performance on specific tasks. Code-specific LLMs are trained on a large corpus of open-source code, such as stack overflow and GitHub, which enables them to write functional and complex code, as shown in Github Copilot and Codeium [3,4].

Given the vast capabilities of LLMs, the work presented in this paper explores the most suitable LLMs and prompt engineering techniques for generating a validation and verification testsuite for high-performance computing (HPC) compilers from a standard specification, which is mainly natural language. More specifically, the goal is to check the correctness of C/C++/Fortran compiler implementations of the directive-based programming models OpenMP [5] and OpenACC [6]. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first of its kind. While this paper focuses on OpenACC, the approach can be adapted to the OpenMP model as well (this is also work in progress). The performance of LLMs on programming tasks such as interview-style questions has been explored over the past couple of years [7]. However, applying this approach to the validation of compilers based on a standard specification has not been explored yet.

Briefly, OpenACC is a directive-based programming model which targets x86 architectures, A64FX and accelerators such as GPUs. OpenACC is defined by a standard specification [6]. Open-source compilers such as GCC [8] and LLVM/Clacc [9], and vendors such as HPE Cray (for Fortran) and NVIDIA, interpret the specification to develop suitable compilers. GCC, Clacc, and HPE Cray compilers target X86, NVIDIA and AMD accelerator architectures, while NVIDIA compilers target X86, NVIDIA GPUs and A64FX architectures. OpenACC offers users varying levels of control over the execution of a program and the flow of data. The model lets the compiler make optimization decisions or allows a customized distribution of data and execution. This is beneficial for domain scientists who do not want to re-implement potentially complex domain applications in a low-level parallel programming language such as CUDA [10], OpenCL [11], or SYCL [12]. OpenACC is a widely popular programming model spanning several domains including climate [13,14,15], computational fluid dynamics [16], nuclear physics [17], and biophysics [18], among others.

## 1.1 Motivation

Given the popularity of the programming model, it is critical that compiler implementations compile and execute the code correctly. Why is this a challenge? Different compiler developers tend to interpret the specification differently, often leading to misinterpretations and ambiguities, and the complexity of the feature definitions is one of several reasons for this. Even with considerable efforts to enhance compilers, they remain prone to issues such as inaccuracy, like all other software [19,20,21,22,23]. Other obvious issues include compilation failures or execution failures that need to be identified and addressed. Also, each compiler implementation offers a different level of support for OpenACC, and coverage of the specification varies too; for example, HPE/Cray supports only Fortran. Nevertheless, the user should not be burdened with these challenges or be expected to tailor their use of the implementations to their applications. The expectation is that the implementations should be the same at the user's level of abstraction.

These challenges directly call for validating the compiler implementations, which can be done by writing functional, corner, regression and stress tests. This can be an involved and recurrent task. We have been developing a validation and verification (V&V) testsuite [24] for OpenACC, just as we have been developing a testsuite for OpenMP [25].

Designing those tests can be quite challenging and cumbersome, and the tests still may not always be correct or complete. There are many ways that the features of the base language (C, C++, or Fortran) and the parallel programming paradigm (OpenACC or OpenMP) can be used together, and it is humanely impossible to cover them all. Tests in both the OpenACC and OpenMP testsuites are created manually, which requires the teams to stay up-to-date with generating and maintaining the tests. Team members change during the project period, and there is a lag when members leave and new members are trained to create quality tests. The lag can range from three weeks to three months or more at times; this observation is based on Chandrasekaran's (co-author) experience training both undergrad and graduate students over a period of 10+ years to work on parallel computing projects. This can harm the project, as we lose continuity and fall behind on deliverable. These hardships motivate this work, which explores the possibility of using LLMs for a V&V testsuite to complement the effort of writing these tests manually.

Developers can then "shift" focus to designing complicated corner case tests and stress testing compiler implementations. LLMs require oversight but can be handy if the effort is front-loaded. LLMs can also help adapt an existing test to new or updated features and perform well at translation between languages. LLMs offer developers many things, though they must be used with human oversight and caution.

This paper makes the following contributions:

- 1. Provides LLM-generated tests to check for correctness of OpenACC compiler implementations

- 2. Explores a fine-tuning dataset for this task

- 3. Evaluates performance of LLMs, prompt engineering techniques, and fine-tuning on test generation for OpenACC

This paper's generated testsuites, prompts, fine-tuning dataset, and specification JSON are available at our GitHub [26].
